<clingo_syntax_reference>

### 1. Rule Structure
Every statement must end with `.`. Three legal forms:
  Fact:       pred(t1,...,tn).
  Rule:       head :- body.
  Constraint: :- body.
Only ONE `:-` per statement — `head :- body1 :- body2` is invalid.
Bare comma-separated atoms without `:-` are invalid:
  Wrong:   input(R, C, V), V != 0.
  Correct: :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

### 2. Aggregates and Choice Rules
Aggregates use braces `{ }`, never parentheses `( )`:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count( R : input(R, _, _) ).

Aggregates always go on the RIGHT side of `=` in an assignment.
As a standalone fact the left side is forbidden:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #min{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     #min{ R : input(R, _, _) } = N.     % aggregate on left of = as a fact

Available aggregates: #count, #sum, #min, #max.

Choice rules guess values within bounds:
  Syntax:   l { atom : condition } u
  Example:  1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

CRITICAL: `{ }` contains exactly ONE atom (optionally followed by `: condition`).
Multiple comma-separated atoms inside `{ }` is illegal:
  Wrong:     1 { R1, C1, V1, R2, C2, V2 : ... } 1
  Correct:   { chosen(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : ... }    % wrap into a single predicate

The terminating `.` goes AFTER the closing `}`, never inside:
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0.}   % `.` inside braces
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0 }.

Conditions after `:` must be predicate literals, never bare constants:
  Wrong:     1 { pattern : 0 } 1      % 0 is a number, not a predicate
  Correct:   1 { pattern : eq(X, 0) } 1   % or use a boolean predicate

### 3. Arithmetic
Modulo is `\`, NOT `#mod`:
  Correct:   (C + L) \ 2 = 0.
  Wrong:     (C + L) #mod 2 = 0.

Operators: +  -  *  /  \  **  |...|

Arithmetic does NOT bind variables. Every variable in an arithmetic expression
must already be grounded by a positive literal elsewhere in the rule body.

### 4. Safety
Every variable must appear in at least one positive (non-negated) predicate in
the rule body. The following do NOT bind variables:
  - `not` (negation)
  - `=`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` (comparisons)
  - `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `\`, `**` (arithmetic)
  - Everything inside `{ }` aggregate or choice braces (Section 6)

Safe example:
  :- input(R, C, V), V != 0, output(R, C, W), W != V.
  % R, C, V bound by input/3; W bound by output/3.

CRITICAL: `not` negates a SINGLE literal, not a parenthesized group.
  Wrong:     :- not (output(R1,C1,V1), input(I,J,V1), used(I,J,R1,C1)).
  Correct:   :- not output(R1,C1,V1).
  (Use separate constraints; `not (a, b, c)` is not valid Clingo.)

Common unsafe patterns and how to fix them:

  1. Variable appears only inside an aggregate:
     Unsafe: rank(R, Rank) :- Rank = #count{X : input(X,C,V), V > R}.
             % R appears only in "V > R" inside the aggregate.
     Safe:   rank(R, Rank) :- input(R,_,_), Rank = #count{X : input(X,C,V), V > R}.

  2. Variable appears only in a choice head (`{ }`), not in the body:
     Unsafe: 1 { pair(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : true } 1 :- true.
     Safe:   1 { pair(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : input(R1,C1,V1), input(R2,C2,V2) } 1.

  3. Variable bound only by `=`, not by a positive predicate:
     Unsafe: allowed(R, C, Color) :- row(R), col(C), Color = V1.
             % V1 is not bound by any predicate.
     Safe:   allowed(R, C, Color) :- condition(C, V1), row(R), col(C), Color = V1.

  4. Variable appears only in arithmetic:
     Unsafe: zero_cell(R,C) :- N - CountC > R, row(R), col(C).
             % N and CountC only appear in arithmetic.
     Safe:   zero_cell(R,C) :- n_rows(N), colCount(C, CountC),
             N - CountC > R, row(R), col(C).
             % N bound by n_rows/1, CountC bound by colCount/2.

### 5. Comparison Predicates
=  !=  <  <=  >  >=
These test values but do NOT bind variables. Variables on both sides must
already be bound by positive literals elsewhere in the rule body.

### 6. Conditions and Conditional Literals
Syntax:  L0 : L1, ..., Ln
ALL variables to the right of `:` are LOCAL to the aggregate — they do NOT
count as positive bindings for the outside of the rule. This includes variables
in condition literals, not just the element term. For example:
  #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0 }
  R, C, and V are ALL local here.  You MUST bind C and V outside the aggregate:
  Unsafe: colCount(C, N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0}.
          % C and Color appear only inside — unsafe.
  Safe:   colCount(C, N) :- row(_), col(C), 
          N = #count{R : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0}.
          % col(C) binds C outside the aggregate.

### 7. #show
Add `#show output/3.` at the end of your program. This hides auxiliary
predicates from the answer set, so only output cells appear in the result.

</clingo_syntax_reference>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Each output cell gets exactly one color
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Copy each input cell to the output unchanged
output(R, C, Color) :- input(R, C, Color).

#show output/3.
</asp>
</example>

### 1. Rule Structure
Every statement must end with `.`. Three legal forms:
  Fact:       pred(t1,...,tn).
  Rule:       head :- body.

Only ONE `:-` per statement — `head :- body1 :- body2` is invalid.
Bare comma-separated atoms without `:-` are invalid:
  Wrong:   input(R, C, V), V != 0.
  Correct: :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

### 2. Aggregates and Choice Rules
Aggregates use braces `{ }`, never parentheses `( )`:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count( R : input(R, _, _) ).

Aggregates always go on the RIGHT side of `=` in an assignment.
As a standalone fact the left side is forbidden:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #min{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     #min{ R : input(R, _, _) } = N.     % aggregate on left of = as a fact

Available aggregates: #count, #sum, #min, #max.

Choice rules guess values within bounds:
  Syntax:   l { atom : condition } u
  Example:  1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

CRITICAL: `{ }` contains exactly ONE atom (optionally followed by `: condition`).
Multiple comma-separated atoms inside `{ }` is illegal:
  Wrong:     1 { R1, C1, V1, R2, C2, V2 : ... } 1
  Correct:   { chosen(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : ... }    % wrap into a single predicate

  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0 }.

Conditions after `:` must be predicate literals, never bare constants:
  Wrong:     1 { pattern : 0 } 1      % 0 is a number, not a predicate
  Correct:   1 { pattern : eq(X, 0) } 1   % or use a boolean predicate

  Wrong:     (C + L) #mod 2 = 0.

Operators: +  -  *  /  \  **  |...|

must already be grounded by a positive literal elsewhere in the rule body.

the rule body. The following do NOT bind variables:

% --------------------------------------------------------------------
%  Grid geometry
% --------------------------------------------------------------------
n_rows(N)    :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(M)    :- M = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(R)       :- n_rows(N), R >= 0, R < N.
col(C)       :- n_cols(M), C >= 0, C < M.
output_cell(R,C) :- row(R), col(C).

% --------------------------------------------------------------------
%  Exactly one colour per output cell
% --------------------------------------------------------------------
1 { output(R, C, Color) : Color } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% --------------------------------------------------------------------
%  Information derived from the input
% --------------------------------------------------------------------
% A colour is present iff it occurs in at least one non‑zero cell.
color(V)      :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Reference cells – one for each colour that occurs in the input.
%  (The puzzles contain exactly two different non‑zero colours.)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
ref(V, R, C)    :- color(V),
                   R = #min{ R1 : input(R1, _, V), V != 0 },
                   C = #min{ C1 : input(R, C1, V), V != 0 },
                   input(R, C, V).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Count non‑zero cells per column – used to decide the direction.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
colCount(C,N)   :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0 }.
colMultipleExists :- colCount(C,N), N >= 2.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Choose the walking direction.
%    orientationRows  – true  ⇔  a column contains ≥2 non‑zero cells
%    (otherwise we walk along the columns)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
orientationRows :- colMultipleExists.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Pick two distinct reference cells (the two colours).
%  The following constraint forces the two reference cells to have
%  different colours – otherwise the model would be rejected.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
:- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2), V1 = V2.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Distance between the two reference cells (rows and columns)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
diffRows(N)    :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2),
                  R2 > R1, N = R2 - R1.

diffCols(N)    :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2),
                  C2 > C1, N = C2 - C1.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  The period of the pattern.
%    – if we walk along rows we use the row distance,
%    – otherwise we use the column distance.
%    period = distance + 2
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
period(P)      :- orientationRows,  P = diffRows + 2.
period(P)      :- not orientationRows, P = diffCols + 2.

% Grid geometry
n_rows(N)    :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(M)    :- M = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(R)       :- n_rows(N), R >= 0, R < N.
col(C)       :- n_cols(M), C >= 0, C < M.

% Reference cells for each non‑zero colour (choose minimal row and column in that row)
ref(V,R,C)    :- color(V), V != 0, row(R), col(C), R = #min{ R0 : input(R0, _, V), V != 0 }, C = #min{ C0 : input(R, C0, V), V != 0 }.

% Two distinct reference cells (choose one for each colour)
% No extra constraint needed; the ref facts already give one per colour

% Orientation predicates
walkRows :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2), C1 = C2.
walkCols :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2), not (C1 = C2).

% Exactly one of walkRows or walkCols must hold
:- walkRows, walkCols.

% Distinct colours
:- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2), V1 = V2.

% Output cell definition
output_cell(R,C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Output the two colours according to the orientation
output(R,C,V1) :- walkRows, R >= R1, (R - R1) \ ((R2 - R1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref(V1,R1,C1,V1).
output(R,C,V2) :- walkRows, R >= R2, (R - R2) \ ((R2 - R1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2).

output(R,C,V1) :- walkCols, C >= C1, (C - C1) \ ((C2 - C1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref(V1,R1,C1,V1).
output(R,C,V2) :- walkCols, C >= C2, (C - C2) \ ((C2 - C1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% Cells not coloured get 0
output(R,C,0) :- output_cell(R,C), not output(R,C,V1), not output(R,C,V2).

% No cell may receive both colours
:- output(R,C,V1), output(R,C,V2).

<context>
You are an expert at solving ARC-AGI (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus) puzzles using Answer Set Programming (ASP).

ARC-AGI puzzles show input-output grid transformations. Each cell contains a color value (integer 0–9). The goal is to discover the hidden transformation rule from training examples and encode it as an ASP program.
</context>

<rules>
- `input(row, col, color)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- `color(0..9)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- the output predicate is always `output(row, col, color)` — do not redefine it.
- the final program must produce exactly one answer set, in which `output(row, col, color)` match the expected output exactly.
</rules>

<clingo_syntax_reference>

### 1. Rule Structure
Every statement must end with `.`. Three legal forms:
  Fact:       pred(t1,...,tn).
  Rule:       head :- body.
  Constraint: :- body.
Only ONE `:-` per statement — `head :- body1 :- body2` is invalid.
Bare comma-separated atoms without `:-` are invalid:
  Wrong:   input(R, C, V), V != 0.
  Correct: :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

### 2. Aggregates and Choice Rules
Aggregates use braces `{ }`, never parentheses `( )`:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count( R : input(R, _, _) ).

Aggregates always go on the RIGHT side of `=` in an assignment.
As a standalone fact the left side is forbidden:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #min{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     #min{ R : input(R, _, _) } = N.     % aggregate on left of = as a fact

Available aggregates: #count, #sum, #min, #max.

Choice rules guess values within bounds:
  Syntax:   l { atom : condition } u
  Example:  1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

CRITICAL: `{ }` contains exactly ONE atom (optionally followed by `: condition`).
Multiple comma-separated atoms inside `{ }` is illegal:
  Wrong:     1 { R1, C1, V1, R2, C2, V2 : ... } 1
  Correct:   { chosen(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : ... }    % wrap into a single predicate

The terminating `.` goes AFTER the closing `}`, never inside:
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0.}   % `.` inside braces
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0 }.

Conditions after `:` must be predicate literals, never bare constants:
  Wrong:     1 { pattern : 0 } 1      % 0 is a number, not a predicate
  Correct:   1 { pattern : eq(X, 0) } 1   % or use a boolean predicate

### 3. Arithmetic
Modulo is `\`, NOT `#mod`:
  Correct:   (C + L) \ 2 = 0.
  Wrong:     (C + L) #mod 2 = 0.

Operators: +  -  *  /  \  **  |...|

Arithmetic does NOT bind variables. Every variable in an arithmetic expression
must already be grounded by a positive literal elsewhere in the rule body.

### 4. Safety
Every variable must appear in at least one positive (non-negated) predicate in
the rule body. The following do NOT bind variables:
  - `not` (negation)
  - `=`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` (comparisons)
  - `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `\`, `**` (arithmetic)
  - Everything inside `{ }` aggregate or choice braces (Section 6)

Safe example:
  :- input(R, C, V), V != 0, output(R, C, W), W != V.
  % R, C, V bound by input/3; W bound by output/3.

CRITICAL: `not` negates a SINGLE literal, not a parenthesized group.
  Wrong:     :- not (output(R1,C1,V1), input(I,J,V1), used(I,J,R1,C1)).
  Correct:   :- not output(R1,C1,V1).
  (Use separate constraints; `not (a, b, c)` is not valid Clingo.)

Common unsafe patterns and how to fix them:

  1. Variable appears only inside an aggregate:
     Unsafe: rank(R, Rank) :- Rank = #count{X : input(X,C,V), V > R}.
             % R appears only in "V > R" inside the aggregate.
     Safe:   rank(R, Rank) :- input(R,_,_), Rank = #count{X : input(X,C,V), V > R}.

  2. Variable appears only in a choice head (`{ }`), not in the body:
     Unsafe: 1 { pair(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : true } 1 :- true.
     Safe:   1 { pair(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : input(R1,C1,V1), input(R2,C2,V2) } 1.

  3. Variable bound only by `=`, not by a positive predicate:
     Unsafe: allowed(R, C, Color) :- row(R), col(C), Color = V1.
             % V1 is not bound by any predicate.
     Safe:   allowed(R, C, Color) :- condition(C, V1), row(R), col(C), Color = V1.

  4. Variable appears only in arithmetic:

output_cell(R,C) :- row(R), col(C).

% --------------------------------------------------------------------

% --------------------------------------------------------------------
% A colour is present iff it occurs in at least one non‑zero cell.
color(V)      :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Reference cells – one for each colour that occurs in the input.
%  (The puzzles contain exactly two different non‑zero colours.)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
ref(V, R, C)    :- color(V),
                   R = #min{ R1 : input(R1, _, V), V != 0 },
                   C = #min{ C1 : input(R, C1, V), V != 0 },
                   input(R, C, V).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Count non‑zero cells per column – used to decide the direction.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
colCount(C,N)   :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0 }.
colMultipleExists :- colCount(C,N), N >= 2.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Choose the walking direction.
%    orientationRows  – true  ⇔  a column contains ≥2 non‑zero cells
%    (otherwise we walk along the columns)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
orientationRows :- colMultipleExists.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Pick two distinct reference cells (the two colours).
%  The following constraint forces the two reference cells to have
%  different colours – otherwise the model would be rejected.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
:- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2), V1 = V2.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
%  Distance between the two reference cells (rows and columns)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------
diffRows(N)    :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2),
                  R2 > R1, N = R2 - R1.

diffCols(N)    :- ref(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref(V2,R2,C2,V2),
                  C2 > C1, N = C2 - C1.

<clingo_syntax_reference>

### 1. Rule Structure
Every statement must end with `.`. Three legal forms:
  Fact:       pred(t1,...,tn).
  Rule:       head :- body.
  Constraint: :- body.
Only ONE `:-` per statement — `head :- body1 :- body2` is invalid.
Bare comma-separated atoms without `:-` are invalid:
  Wrong:   input(R, C, V), V != 0.
  Correct: :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

### 2. Aggregates and Choice Rules
Aggregates use braces `{ }`, never parentheses `( )`:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count( R : input(R, _, _) ).

Aggregates always go on the RIGHT side of `=` in an assignment.
As a standalone fact the left side is forbidden:
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #min{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
  Wrong:     #min{ R : input(R, _, _) } = N.     % aggregate on left of = as a fact

Available aggregates: #count, #sum, #min, #max.

Choice rules guess values within bounds:
  Syntax:   l { atom : condition } u
  Example:  1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

CRITICAL: `{ }` contains exactly ONE atom (optionally followed by `: condition`).
Multiple comma-separated atoms inside `{ }` is illegal:
  Wrong:     1 { R1, C1, V1, R2, C2, V2 : ... } 1
  Correct:   { chosen(R1,C1,V1,R2,C2,V2) : ... }    % wrap into a single predicate

The terminating `.` goes AFTER the closing `}`, never inside:
  Wrong:     val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0.}   % `.` inside braces
  Correct:   val(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, C, V), V != 0 }.

Conditions after `:` must be predicate literals, never bare constants:
  Wrong:     1 { pattern : 0 } 1      % 0 is a number, not a predicate
  Correct:   1 { pattern : eq(X, 0) } 1   % or use a boolean predicate

### 3. Arithmetic
Modulo is `\`, NOT `#mod`:
  Correct:   (C + L) \ 2 = 0.
  Wrong:     (C + L) #mod 2 = 0.

Operators: +  -  *  /  \  **  |...|

Arithmetic does NOT bind variables. Every variable in an arithmetic expression
must already be grounded by a positive literal elsewhere in the rule body.

### 4. Safety
Every variable must appear in at least one positive (non-negated) predicate in
the rule body. The following do NOT bind variables:
  - `not` (negation)
  - `=`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` (comparisons)
  - `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `\`, `**` (arithmetic)
  - Everything inside `{ }` aggregate or choice braces (Section 6)

  % R, C, V bound by input/3; W bound by output/3.

CRITICAL: `not` negates a SINGLE literal, not a parenthesized group.
  Wrong:     :- not (output(R1,C1,V1), input(I,J,V1), used(I,J,R1,C1)).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------

% Colors (non‑zero)
color(V) :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

% Reference cell for colour V1 (smaller colour)
ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1) :- color(V1), input(R1, C1, V1), R1 = #min{R0 : input(R0, _, V1)}, C1 = #min{C0 : input(R1, C0, V1)}.

% Reference cell for colour V2 (larger colour)
ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2) :- color(V2), input(R2, C2, V2), R2 = #min{R0 : input(R0, _, V2)}, C2 = #min{C0 : input(R2, C0, V2)}.

% Same column orientation (the two colours lie in the same column)
sameCol :- ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2), C1 = C2.

% Same row orientation (the two colours lie in the same row)
sameRow :- ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2), R1 = R2.

% Every cell (R,C) is a potential output cell
output_cell(R,C) :- input(R, _, _), input(_, C, _).

% Output when the two colours share a column (pattern walks vertically)
output(R,C,V1) :- sameCol, (R - R1) \ ((R2 - R1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

output(R,C,V2) :- sameCol, (R - R2) \ ((R2 - R1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% Output when the two colours share a row (pattern walks horizontally)
output(R,C,V1) :- sameRow, (C - C1) \ ((C2 - C1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

output(R,C,V2) :- sameRow, (C - C2) \ ((C2 - C1) + 2) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% Cells that receive no colour become 0
output(R,C,0) :- output_cell(R,C), not output(R,C,V1), not output(R,C,V2), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% No cell may contain both colours
:- output(R,C,V1), output(R,C,V2).

% The two colours must be ordered: the smaller colour is V1
:- V1 < V2.

% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(M) :- M = #count{C : input(_, C, _) }.

% Dummy predicates for safety
dummy_row(R) :- true.
dummy_col(C) :- true.

% Rows and columns with bounds
row(R) :- n_rows(N), R >= 0, R < N, dummy_row(R).
col(C) :- n_cols(M), C >= 0, C < M, dummy_col(C).

% Output cells
output_cell(R,C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Non‑zero colors
color(V) :- input(R, C, V), V != 0.

% Two distinct colors
color(V1), color(V2), V1 != V2.

% Reference cells for each color
ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1) :- color(V1), input(R1, C1, V1), R1 = #min{R0 : input(R0, _, V1), V1 != 0}, C1 = #min{C0 : input(R1, C0, V1), V1 != 0}.
ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2) :- color(V2), input(R2, C2, V2), R2 = #min{R0 : input(R0, _, V2), V2 != 0}, C2 = #min{C0 : input(R2, C0, V2), V2 != 0}.

% Same column (both colors in the same column)
sameCol :- ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2), C1 = C2.

% Max and min rows and columns of the two colors
maxRow(N) :- N = #max{R0 : color(V), input(R0, _, V)}.
minRow(M) :- M = #min{R0 : color(V), input(R0, _, V)}.
maxCol(N) :- N = #max{C0 : input(_, C0, V), color(V)}.
minCol(M) :- M = #min{C0 : input(_, C0, V), color(V)}.

% Period based on orientation
period(P) :- sameCol, maxRow(N), minRow(M), P = (N - M) * 2.
period(P) :- not sameCol, maxCol(N), minCol(M), P = (N - M) * 2.

% Enforce order V1 < V2 using the already defined period
:- period(P), V1 < V2.

% Output when colors share a column
output(R,C,V1) :- sameCol, (R - R1) \ period(P) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).
output(R,C,V2) :- sameCol, (R - R2) \ period(P) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% Output when colors are in different columns
output(R,C,V1) :- not sameCol, (C - C1) \ period(P) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).
output(R,C,V2) :- not sameCol, (C - C2) \ period(P) = 0, output_cell(R,C), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% Zero cells for the remaining cells
output(R,C,0) :- output_cell(R,C), not output(R,C,V1), not output(R,C,V2), ref1(V1,R1,C1,V1), ref2(V2,R2,C2,V2).

% At most one color per cell
:- output(R,C,V1), output(R,C,V2).

% Show only output facts
#show output/3.
